extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and readers interested in research integrity and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Detecting and evaluating signs that a manuscript's editorial handling or peer review was compromised (including paper-mill activity in special/guest-edited issues) and determining when such concerns justify corrective action such as retraction. The page reports specific grounds cited in retraction notices and procedural practices publishers invoke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromised editorial handling and peer review process
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher's investigation found 'compromised editorial handling and peer review process.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is cited as a direct ground for retraction: when editorial workflows or the integrity of peer review are compromised (e.g., improper acceptance, manipulated reviewer suggestions, or other malpractice), the publisher may no longer have confidence in the article's results and conclusions and retract it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate or irrelevant references
rubrics_metrics.description: The retraction notices list 'inappropriate or irrelevant references' among the concerns for affected articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of references that do not properly support the work or appear irrelevant can indicate poor scholarship or citation manipulation (potentially tied to paper mills) and is a substantive reason to question the article's validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article not in scope of journal or guest-edited issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices state some articles were 'not being in scope of the journal or guest-edited issue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Out-of-scope submissions accepted into a journal or special issue suggest failures in editorial screening or misuse of guest-edited issue processes; such scope mismatch can contribute to retraction decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of author response to correspondence regarding retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted in retraction notices that 'The authors have not responded to correspondence regarding this retraction' or authors 'have not responded' or 'have not stated whether they agree or disagree.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure of authors to engage with publisher correspondence during an investigation is recorded in notices and may affect the process and final decision; publishers typically attempt to contact authors before retracting but may proceed if there's no satisfactory response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation following established processes and COPE guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: A Springer Nature spokesperson stated investigations are carried out 'following an established process and in line with best-practice COPE guidelines.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When concerns arise, publishers should investigate carefully, follow standard procedural safeguards (e.g., COPE guidance), and consult relevant editorial leadership before issuing retractions or other notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation with Editor-in-Chief and loss of confidence in results/conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction decisions are made 'in agreement with the Editor-in-Chief' and when the publisher 'no longer has confidence in the results and conclusions of this article.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers typically consult editorial leadership (EIC) and, if the investigation undermines confidence in the integrity or validity of findings, will retract the article. Loss of confidence is the practical threshold cited for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special/guest-edited issues are particularly vulnerable to paper mills
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes 'Special issues have emerged over the past few years as particularly vulnerable to paper mills' and gives examples of guest-edited issues being 'hacked by publication cheats.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special issues require heightened scrutiny because guest-editing workflows can be exploited; publishers and editors should audit these issues, verify guest-editor practices, and apply extra checks to detect paper-mill activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial accountability for acceptance decisions (guest editors vs appointed editors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters discuss that guest editors can and do accept papers and that 'an irresponsible editor can accept the recommendation of a guest without checking the contents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility for acceptance decisions lies with the editors who oversee the process; journals should clarify roles and ensure appointed editors or EICs verify guest-editor recommendations to prevent acceptance without proper review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternatives to retraction and fairness to authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple commenters argue authors should be given a chance to respond and that journals should consider corrections rather than immediately retracting papers, or hold guest/handling editors accountable instead of penalizing authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should consider proportional remedies, document author communication, and weigh corrective options (correction, expression of concern) where appropriate; transparency and fair treatment of authors are important ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of publisher-level identification and action for papers of concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher statement: 'These papers were identified as part of our ongoing commitment to identifying and acting on papers of concern.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers are expected to proactively identify problematic papers (e.g., via audits, whistleblowing, or post-publication review) and take appropriate corrective actions following investigation and policy, signaling institutional responsibility for maintaining the literature's integrity.
